area: Area I. Pilot Privileges and Currency
objective: By the end of this lesson you can read a logbook and say, with the rule behind it, whether a pilot may carry passengers by day, carry them at night, or act as pilot in command under IFR today, and what it takes to get current again.
why: Currency rules are easy to half-remember after a break, and a wrong guess means flying illegally with people aboard or in the clouds. Knowing the exact rule, and the gap between current and proficient, keeps you legal and safe.

prereading.what: Recent flight experience: 90-day passenger and night rules, instrument experience, the instrument proficiency check and the exceptions.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 61.57(a) to (e)

prereading.what: Pilot logbooks: what to record, logging PIC, SIC, instrument and training time, and device time for currency.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 61.51(a) to (i)

prereading.what: Safety pilot rules for simulated instrument flight, and throwover control wheels.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.109

prereading.what: FAA guidance on recent general experience, night currency, make and model, and using simulators and ATDs for IFR currency.
prereading.label: AC 61-98E Ch 3, 3-1 to 3-2

prereading.what: How an instrument proficiency check is structured, who can give it, and what devices may be used.
prereading.label: AC 61-98E Ch 5, 5-1 to 5-3

prereading.what: Six steps to set personal minimums, including the extra margin for lack of currency.
prereading.label: RMH Ch 2, 2-1 to 2-5

warmup: Your logbook shows "3 night landings" from 70 days ago. Can you take a friend on a night flight tonight? What else would you need to check in those entries before you say yes?

key_terms.def: The 61.57 minimums you must have done lately to act as PIC with persons aboard, at night, or under IFR.
You alone flew the airplane. Landings someone else flew do not count for your currency.
A landing where the airplane stops on the runway before the next takeoff. Needed for tailwheel and night currency.
For night passenger currency: the period from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise.
End of evening civil twilight to beginning of morning civil twilight. Used for logging night time.
A whole month, first day to last. The IFR window is the 6 calendar months before the month of the flight.
A check using the Instrument Rating ACS areas; the only way back once you have been out of IFR currency for more than 6 calendar months.
A pilot in the other control seat during simulated instrument flight, with at least a private certificate for that category and class.
A hood or similar device that blocks your outside view so you fly by instruments only.
An FAA-approved training device other than a FFS or FTD. Its Letter of Authorization says what credit it gives.

chunks.title: Three clocks: passengers, night and IFR

body.p: 14 CFR 61.57 sets the recent flight experience you need to act as pilot in command (PIC). Pilots call it currency. It runs three separate clocks, and each one controls a different privilege [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57]].

head: To do this as PIC
You need
Look-back window
rows: 3 takeoffs and 3 landings as sole manipulator, same category, class and type (if a class or type rating is required); full stops in a tailwheel airplane if you will fly one [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)]]
Carry persons from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise
3 takeoffs and 3 landings to a full stop in that same period, sole manipulator, same category, class and type [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]]
Fly under IFR, or in weather below VFR minimums
6 instrument approaches, holding procedures and tasks, and intercepting and tracking courses with navigation systems [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]]
6 calendar months before the month of the flight
Get back after more than 6 more calendar months out of IFR currency

body.p: Currency is not the flight review. The flight review is its own rule: no PIC without a satisfactory flight review in the preceding 24 calendar months [[15:23|AC 61-98E 4.1.2.1]].

callout.text: Common mistake: "biennial flight review" is an old name. The FAA now says "flight review," because the old term implied you only needed training once every 24 months [[15:5|AC 61-98E 1.7.1]].

body.p: All of these are minimums. The FAA asks pilots to build a personal currency program that goes beyond what 14 CFR requires [[15:7|AC 61-98E 1.9.1]].

check.q: You made 3 day landings last week but none at night in 4 months. Can you take a friend flying by day? At night?
check.a: By day, yes, if the landings were in the same category and class [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)]]. From 1 hour after sunset, no, not until you make 3 full-stop night takeoffs and landings [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]].

body.p: The rule: no person may act as PIC of an aircraft carrying persons, or of an aircraft certificated for more than one pilot, unless they made at least three takeoffs and three landings within the preceding 90 days [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)]]. In practice:

bullets: You must be the sole manipulator of the flight controls. Landings your instructor or a friend flew do not count [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)(i)]].

Same category, class and type (if a class or type rating is required). Airplane single-engine land landings count for any single-engine land airplane that needs no type rating [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)(ii)]].
Make and model is not part of the rule for small, non-high-performance airplanes. Landings in a Cessna 152 count for a Cessna 172 [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.3]].
Flying a tailwheel airplane? The three landings must be to a full stop, in a tailwheel airplane [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)(ii)]].

head: Way to get current
What the rule says
rows: For the purpose of meeting (a)(1), you may act as PIC under day VFR or day IFR with no persons or property aboard except those needed for the flight [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(2)]]

(a) and (b) do not apply to training limited to meeting them, if you meet all other PIC requirements and you and the instructor are the only occupants [[60:241|14 CFR 61.57(e)(5)]] [[60:242|14 CFR 61.57(e)(5)(ii)-(iii)]]
Only a FFS or FTD approved for landings, used in an approved course at a Part 142 training center [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(3)]]

callout.text: Common mistake: tailwheel touch-and-goes. For a nosewheel airplane the rule does not ask for full stops, but for passengers in a tailwheel airplane all three landings must be full stops in a tailwheel airplane [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)(ii)]].

body.p: Pilots flying for a Part 121, 125 or 135 certificate holder meet that part's rules instead, but only while flying for that certificate holder. Rent a light airplane on your day off and 61.57 applies to you like anyone else [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(e)(1)-(3)]].

check.q: You fly a nosewheel Cessna 172 and a tailwheel Citabria. In the last 90 days you made 5 touch-and-goes in the Citabria and nothing in the 172. Can you take a passenger in either one?
check.a: In the 172, yes: same category and class, and nosewheel currency does not need full stops. In the Citabria, no: tailwheel currency needs full-stop landings [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)(ii)]].

body.p: The rule: no person may act as PIC of an aircraft carrying persons from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise, unless within the preceding 90 days they made at least three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop during that same period [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]]. You must be the sole manipulator, in the same category, class and type (if required) [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)(i)-(ii)]].

head: Rule
"Night" means
Used for
rows: End of evening civil twilight to beginning of morning civil twilight [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]]
1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]]
Night passenger currency, and the landings that earn it

body.p: Evening civil twilight starts at sunset and ends when the center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon [[24:218|AFH 11-1]]. So the 61.57(b) window usually starts later than night for logging.

callout.text: Common mistake: logged night is not night currency. A landing after civil twilight ends but before 1 hour after sunset can go in the night column, yet it does not count toward 61.57(b). And every night currency landing must be a full stop, in any airplane [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]] [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]].

body.p: The restriction covers only that window. Land with a passenger before 1 hour after sunset and night currency is not required, though your position lights must be on from sunset [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]] [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)(1)]]. A FFS counts only if approved for takeoffs and landings, with the visual set to night, in a Part 142 course [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(b)(2)]].

When you go get those landings: height and sink rate are harder to judge at night, and inexperienced pilots tend to round out too high. Hold a constant descent until the landing light shows tire marks, then round out [[24:228|AFH 11-11]]. A VASI is an indispensable aid for the glide path [[24:227|AFH 11-10]].

check.q: Sunset is 1830. From what time do your takeoffs and landings count toward night passenger currency?
check.a: From 1930, 1 hour after sunset, and each landing must be to a full stop [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]].

body.p: The rule: you may act as PIC under IFR, or in weather below VFR minimums, only if within the 6 calendar months before the month of the flight you performed and logged, in actual weather or under simulated conditions using a view-limiting device [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]]:

bullets: Six instrument approaches.
Holding procedures and tasks.
Intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigational electronic systems [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)(i)-(iii)]].

body.p: The tasks must be done in an aircraft appropriate to the instrument privileges you want to keep, so airplane IFR needs airplane tasks or a device that represents airplanes [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)-(2)]].

**Devices.** You may do the tasks in a full flight simulator (FFS), flight training device (FTD) or aviation training device (ATD) if it represents the aircraft category and you fly them in simulated instrument conditions. Any combination of aircraft and devices is allowed [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(2)]].

bullets: A FFS or FTD must be qualified and approved by the FAA for the credit you take [[60:194|14 CFR 61.4(a)]] [[15:21|AC 61-98E 3.2]].
An ATD gives the currency credit its FAA Letter of Authorization (LOA) lists for that model [[15:21|AC 61-98E 3.2]].
No instructor has to be present for currency. Keep a logbook or training record of the device, the time and the content [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(5)]].

callout.text: Common mistake: thinking device time and airplane time cannot be mixed. Today's 61.57(c)(2) says you may complete the instrument experience in any combination of an aircraft, FFS, FTD and ATD. If you learned older limits on mixing them, go by the current text [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(2)]].

body.p: Holding is a required task, so fly real entries and timing. Standard pattern: inbound to the fix, right turns, and 1-minute inbound legs at or below 14,000 ft [[23:301|IFH 10-10]].

check.q: In the window you flew 6 ILS approaches with a safety pilot, but no holding. Are you IFR current?
check.a: No. The rule needs all three: six approaches, holding procedures and tasks, and intercepting and tracking [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]].

chunks.title: Count the months: catch-up window and IPC

body.p: The IFR window is counted in calendar months back from the month of the flight [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]]. Tasks finished anytime in March cover a flight on September 30, because September's window is March through August.

head: Last tasks done in March. Month of flight:
PIC under IFR?
What to do
rows: Keep the tasks rolling forward [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]]
Catch up: do the tasks with a safety pilot, an instructor or a device [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]]
Out more than six calendar months: only an IPC restores currency [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]]

callout.text: Common mistake: the "6-month grace period" is not time you may fly IFR. In those months you may not act as PIC under IFR or below VFR minimums; it is only a window to catch up without an IPC [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]] [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]].

body.p: **The IPC.** It must include the areas of operation of the Instrument Rating ACS, as listed in appendix A of Part 61 [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]]. It may be in an aircraft of the right category, or in a FFS or FTD that represents it [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(2)]]. It may be given by [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(3)]]:

bullets: An examiner, or a person approved by the FAA to give instrument practical tests.
An authorized instructor. The instructor must hold an instrument rating on both the pilot and the flight instructor certificate for the category and class used [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]].
A Part 121, 125, 135 or 91K company check pilot, if both of you work for that operator.
A U.S. Armed Forces examiner, for members of the Armed Forces.

body.p: All or part of an IPC may be done in a FFS, FTD or ATD, but only an advanced ATD (AATD) may be used, and only for the credit its LOA allows [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.2]]. The instructor may add any maneuver needed to see that you can operate safely under IFR [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.3]].

callout.text: Changed: the IFH describes the IPC as an inflight evaluation by an instrument instructor using PTS tasks [[23:11|IFH viii]]. Today's rule points to the Instrument Rating ACS, allows a FFS or FTD, and also lists examiners and check pilots [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)]].

check.q: All your instrument tasks were in January. It is now August. What do you need before flying IFR?
check.a: January covered flights through July. In August you are out of currency but not by more than six calendar months, so just complete the six approaches, holding and tracking. No IPC yet [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]] [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]].

chunks.title: Logging: what the record must show

body.p: You must record the experience you use to meet recent flight experience requirements [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(a)(2)]]. If it is not logged, it does not prove currency.

head: Record
What to enter
rows: Date; total time; where you departed and arrived (or where a device lesson took place); type and ID of aircraft or device; safety pilot's name if 91.109 required one [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(b)(1)]]
Solo, PIC, SIC, training received from an instructor, device training [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(b)(2)]] [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(b)(2)(v)]]
Day or night; actual instrument; simulated instrument in flight or in a device [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(b)(3)]]
Location and type of each approach, and the safety pilot's name if required [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(3)]]
The training device, the time and the content [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(5)]]

body.p: **Instrument time.** Log it only while you operate the aircraft solely by reference to instruments, in actual or simulated conditions [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(1)]]. An instructor may log it while giving instrument instruction in actual conditions [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(2)]].

**PIC time.** A private, commercial or ATP pilot may log PIC as sole manipulator of the controls of an aircraft they are rated for, as sole occupant, or while acting as PIC where the type certificate or the regulations require more than one pilot [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(e)(1)]].
**Training time.** The instructor endorses it legibly with a description, the length, signature, certificate number and expiration date or recent experience end date [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(h)(2)]].

callout.text: Common mistake: thinking a sim session needs a CFI to count. For a new certificate or rating, an instructor must be present and sign (61.51(g)(4)). For currency, a record of the device, time and content is enough (61.51(g)(5)) [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(4)-(5)]].

body.p: On reasonable request you must show your logbook to the FAA, the NTSB or a law enforcement officer [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(1)]].

check.q: What must your logbook show for each approach flown in the airplane that you count for IFR currency?
check.a: The location and type of each approach, and the name of the safety pilot if one was required [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(3)]].

body.p: The rule: no person may operate a civil aircraft in simulated instrument flight unless the other control seat holds a safety pilot [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]]. The requirements:

bullets: At least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings for the aircraft. The rule does not ask for an instrument rating [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)(i)]].
Adequate vision forward and to each side, or a competent observer aboard who supplements it [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]].

Fully functioning dual controls. A single-engine airplane with a throwover wheel is allowed only if the safety pilot decides the flight is safe and the pilot flying holds at least a private certificate with category and class ratings [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(3)]].

Because 91.109(c) requires the safety pilot, treat them as a required pilot flight crewmember: 61.3(c)(1) then calls for an appropriate medical certificate or other documentation acceptable to the FAA [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(c)(1)]].

body.p: **Who is PIC?** Decide before takeoff. The rated pilot under the hood may log PIC as sole manipulator [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(e)(1)(i)]]. Because the regulations require a second pilot for this flight, the safety pilot may log SIC if they hold the category and class ratings (and an instrument rating if the flight needs one) [[60:229|14 CFR 61.51(f)(2)]]. If the safety pilot acts as PIC, they may log PIC [[60:228|14 CFR 61.51(e)(1)(iii)]]. Whoever is PIC must be current for what the flight involves: persons aboard, night or IFR [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57]].

callout.text: Pick weather good enough to make up for the safety pilot's restricted view and your focus on the panel, with extra margin near busy airways and airports [[33:258|AIM 4-3-16c]]. Brief the three-step exchange of controls: a verbal handoff by the pilot flying, verbal acceptance by the pilot taking over, and a verbal and visual confirmation by the pilot giving up control [[15:9|AC 61-98E 2.1.1]].

body.p: Under the hood, the instructor or safety pilot has to keep looking for traffic through every phase of the flight [[15:31|AC 61-98E 5.1.3.1]].

check.q: Your friend holds a private certificate, airplane single-engine land, with no instrument rating. Can she be your safety pilot in a Cessna 172 with dual controls?
check.a: Yes. 91.109(c) needs a private pilot with the category and class ratings, adequate vision and dual controls. No instrument rating is required [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]] [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)-(3)]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: read the logbook, decide today

body.p: Work in the same order every time, starting from today's date and the flight you want to make.

bullets: 1. Write down what the flight involves: persons aboard? Any part of it from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise? IFR or below VFR minimums [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)-(b)]] [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]]?

2. Passengers: count back 90 days. Find 3 takeoffs and 3 landings you flew as sole manipulator, same category, class and type (if required). Tailwheel: full stops in a tailwheel airplane [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)]].

3. Night: in those 90 days, find 3 takeoffs and 3 full-stop landings made from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise. A night-column entry alone may not prove it; check times or remarks [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]] [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]].

4. IFR: list the 6 calendar months before this month. Count approaches (with location and type logged), holding, and intercepting and tracking, in the airplane or an approved device [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]] [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(3)]].
5. Short on IFR? Out more than six calendar months past the window: IPC. Otherwise finish the tasks with a safety pilot, an instructor or a device [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]].

6. Then the rest of PIC: a flight review within 24 calendar months [[15:23|AC 61-98E 4.1.2.1]] and your medical certificate, or BasicMed [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(c)(1)]] [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(c)(2)(xiii)]].
7. Last, compare the flight with your personal minimums, adjusted for how recent your experience is [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

body.p: The RMH experience summary puts your recent experience on one page: landings, night landings, IFR hours and approaches in the last 12 months [[30:14|RMH 2-2]]. Before an IPC, AC 61-98E Appendix G does the same for instrument time, including approaches in the last 6 months [[15:44|AC 61-98E G-1]].

check.q: Today is October 20. Your last six approaches, holding and tracking were all in April. Can you act as PIC under IFR today?
check.a: Yes. The window for an October flight is April through September, so the April tasks still count [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]].

body.p: Treat 61.57(a) and (b) as minimums. A pilot current only in light winds at long runways should get more takeoff and landing practice in strong winds or on short runways before carrying passengers in those conditions [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.1]]. Night experience is usually a small part of total time, so think hard about extra practice and planning before marginal weather at night [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.2]].

bullets: Loss of control usually happens when pilots lack proficiency [[15:9|AC 61-98E 2.1.2]].
Pilots who are instrument rated but not instrument proficient are susceptible to spatial disorientation and loss of control in IMC [[15:12|AC 61-98E 2.1.5]].
The instrument rating does not by itself make you a competent all-weather pilot [[23:11|IFH viii]].
Accident rates go up for pilots with little or no time in the type flown. Get a checkout in each make and model [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.3]].

body.p: **Personal minimums.** The RMH builds them in six steps: know the weather categories, assess your experience and comfort level, add wind and performance limits, assemble a baseline, adjust for the conditions, and stick to the plan [[30:13|RMH 2-1]] [[30:16|RMH 2-4]] [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].
Lack of currency, such as not flying for several weeks, is a pilot factor. The RMH sample margin is to add at least 500 feet to your ceiling minimum [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].
Don't adjust minimums to make a specific flight happen. Change one value at a time, and talk to an instructor before a big change [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

callout.text: Currency answers "May I?" Proficiency answers "Should I?" Legal is the floor, not the plan.

check.q: Your baseline night VFR ceiling is 5,000 ft. You haven't flown in 7 weeks. Using the RMH sample margin, what ceiling do you want tonight?
check.a: At least 5,500 ft: add at least 500 ft for lack of currency [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

bullets: Counting landings someone else flew. You must be the sole manipulator [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)(i)]].
Counting tailwheel touch-and-goes for tailwheel passenger currency [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)(ii)]].
Using sunset or the end of civil twilight instead of 1 hour after sunset for night currency landings [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]].
Night touch-and-goes. Night currency needs full stops [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]].
Counting six months from a date instead of 6 calendar months before the month of the flight [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]].
Flying IFR during the catch-up months [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]].
Six approaches but no holding or tracking [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]].
Not logging the location and type of each approach, or the safety pilot's name [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(3)]].
A safety pilot without a private certificate and the right category and class [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]].
Taking ATD credit its LOA does not give [[15:21|AC 61-98E 3.2]].

check.q: A friend says you have six months of "grace" to keep flying IFR after your currency runs out. Is that right?
check.a: No. In those months you may not act as PIC under IFR. You can only regain currency without an IPC [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]].

External pressures: deadlines or passenger pressure, subtract at least 5 knots from winds.

Turbulence for single-engine and multiengine: surface wind 10 and 15 knots, gusts 5 and 8 knots, crosswind 7 and 7. Performance: shortest runway 2,500 and 4,500 ft, highest terrain 6,000 and 3,000 ft, highest density altitude 3,000 and 3,000 ft.

scenario.title: Thirteen months away, and a low-ceiling Saturday
scenario.setup: You hold a commercial pilot certificate, airplane single-engine land, with an instrument rating. A new job kept you out of the airplane for 13 months. Your last approaches, holding and tracking were in February of last year, and you were fully current then. Today is March 3. You want to take your sister IFR on Saturday to a coastal airport forecast at 600 ft overcast and 2 miles in mist. Your flying club's AATD and an instrument instructor are free on Thursday.

questions.q: What do you need before you may act as PIC under IFR?
questions.a: An IPC. February's tasks covered flights through August. From September you were out of currency, and by March you have been out for more than six calendar months, so only an instrument proficiency check restores it [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]] [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]].

questions.q: Can Thursday's AATD session be your IPC?
questions.a: Partly. All or part of an IPC may be done in an approved device, but only an AATD may be used, and only for the credit its LOA gives; the instructor plans the rest [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.2]]. The rule itself allows an aircraft of the right category or a FFS or FTD [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(2)]].

questions.q: You also haven't landed in 13 months. Can your sister ride along Saturday?
questions.a: Only after you make 3 takeoffs and 3 landings as sole manipulator in a single-engine land airplane within 90 days. Do them solo before Saturday, or with an instructor in training aimed only at getting current, with just the two of you aboard [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)]] [[60:242|14 CFR 61.57(e)(5)]].

questions.q: You pass the IPC on Friday. Is 600 ft and 2 miles on Saturday a good idea?
questions.a: Legal is not the same as proficient. Lack of currency is a reason to add at least 500 ft to your ceiling minimum, and you should not lower minimums to make a trip happen [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. Instrument-rated pilots who are not proficient are susceptible to loss of control in IMC [[15:12|AC 61-98E 2.1.5]]. Pick a better day, or an alternate plan.

questions.q: How do you keep from ending up here again?
questions.a: Build a personal currency program that goes beyond 14 CFR minimums, folding approaches and landings into normal flights [[15:7|AC 61-98E 1.9.1]]. Set instrument goals, such as how often to fly IFR each month, with the AC 61-98E Appendix H plan [[15:45|AC 61-98E H-1]].

skills.do: Given a logbook page, a date and a planned flight, say whether the pilot may carry passengers by day, carry them from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise, and act as PIC under IFR, point to the entries that prove each answer, and say what it would take to get current.
skills.practice: Before a flight review or IPC, fill in the RMH experience summary or the AC 61-98E Appendix G summary from your own logbook [[30:14|RMH 2-2]] [[15:44|AC 61-98E G-1]]. Then run the 90-day, night and 6-calendar-month checks out loud for three dates: today, 30 days from now and 90 days from now [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)-(b)]] [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]].

quiz.q: To carry a passenger in a nosewheel Cessna 172, which landings from the past 90 days count?
options: 3 takeoffs and landings you flew in any airplane single-engine land
3 landings your instructor flew while you were aboard
3 landings in any category of aircraft, if one was a full stop
3 landings in a home flight simulator program
quiz.why: You must be the sole manipulator, in the same category and class [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)]]. For small non-high-performance airplanes, make and model does not matter for the rule [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.3]].

quiz.q: For passenger currency in a tailwheel airplane, the three landings must be:
options: At night, between sunset and sunrise
With an instructor aboard
To a full stop, in a tailwheel airplane
In the same make and model
quiz.why: If the airplane to be flown has a tailwheel, the takeoffs and landings must be to a full stop in a tailwheel airplane [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)(ii)]].

quiz.q: Sunset is 1900. From what time do landings count toward night passenger currency?
options: 1900, at sunset
1930, about the end of civil twilight
2000, 1 hour after sunset
2100, 2 hours after sunset
quiz.why: 61.57(b) uses the period from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]]. The end of civil twilight is the 14 CFR 1.1 night used for logging [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]].

quiz.q: Your last instrument tasks were all done in May. Through what month may you act as PIC under IFR?
options: October
November
August
December
quiz.why: For a November flight the window is May through October, so May still counts. For December the window starts in June [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]].

quiz.q: The same pilot (last tasks in May) does nothing more. When is an IPC first required?
options: June 1 of the next year
December 1
May 1 of the next year
Never, as long as a safety pilot flies along
quiz.why: Currency ends November 30. December through May is six calendar months out; in June it is more than six, so only an IPC restores currency [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]].

quiz.q: What is the minimum certificate for a safety pilot in a Cessna 172?
options: An instrument rating on any pilot certificate
A CFII certificate
A student pilot certificate with a solo endorsement
A private pilot certificate with airplane single-engine land
quiz.why: The safety pilot needs at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings for the aircraft [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)(i)]].

quiz.q: For approaches flown in the airplane to count for IFR currency, your logbook must show:
options: Only the total number of approaches
The location and type of each approach, and the safety pilot's name if required
An instructor's endorsement for each approach
The ATIS code and the altimeter setting for each approach
quiz.why: 61.51(g)(3) requires the location and type of each approach and the safety pilot's name, if required [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(3)]].

quiz.q: You fly approaches, holding and tracking alone in an ATD. What makes them count for currency?
options: An instructor must be present and sign your logbook
They count only as part of an IPC
The ATD is used as its LOA allows, and you record the device, time and content
They never count; only aircraft time counts
quiz.why: ATD currency credit is as specified in the device's LOA [[15:21|AC 61-98E 3.2]], and for currency you need a record of the device, time and content [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(5)]].

quiz.q: In the RMH sample margins (Figure 2-9), which adjustment goes with a pilot factor like not having flown for several weeks?
options: Add at least 1/2 mile to visibility
Subtract at least 5 knots from winds
Add at least 500 feet to runway length
Add at least 500 feet to the ceiling
quiz.why: The Pilot row (illness, medication, stress, fatigue, lack of currency) pairs with adding at least 500 feet to the ceiling [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

quiz.q: Which of these may NOT give an instrument proficiency check?
options: An authorized instructor
An examiner
A private pilot with an instrument rating
A Part 135 check pilot, for a pilot at the same company
quiz.why: 61.57(d)(3) lists an examiner, an Armed Forces examiner, a company check pilot (both employees), an authorized instructor, or a person approved by the FAA [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(3)]].

takeaways: Passengers: 3 takeoffs and landings in 90 days, sole manipulator, same category and class; tailwheel needs full stops.
Night passengers: 3 full-stop takeoffs and landings from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise.
IFR: 6 approaches, holding, and intercepting and tracking in the 6 calendar months before the month of the flight.
The catch-up months are not permission to fly IFR. Out more than six calendar months: IPC only.
Log approach location and type and the safety pilot's name; for devices, log the device, time and content.
Safety pilot: private certificate with category and class, good vision, dual controls.
Current is legal, not proficient. Raise your personal minimums after a break.
cfi_notes: Pilots back from a break often think "6 months" means 180 days. Have them count calendar months on a real calendar for three dates.

The IFH (p. viii) describes the IPC as an inflight evaluation using PTS tasks and says "within the preceding 6 months." Teach 61.57(c) and (d) as written: calendar months, the Instrument Rating ACS, and FFS/FTD (and AATD per AC 61-98E 5.1.2) allowed.
AC 61-98E Appendix I quotes an older wording of 61.57(d) ("flight simulator," "must consist of"). Use the current eCFR text.
AC 61-98E 5.2.1 still says "Airport/Facility Directory (A/FD)" [[15:32|AC 61-98E 5.2.1]]; that publication is now the Chart Supplement U.S. [[1:337|PHAK 14-3]].
Instructors and examiners commonly probe: logged night vs night currency, tailwheel full stops, whether watching from the right seat counts, and who is PIC with a safety pilot.

Safety pilot logging (SIC under 61.51(f)(2), PIC under 61.51(e)(1)(iii)) and the medical point (61.3(c)) are read from the rule text. FAA legal interpretations on them are not in the course sources; point pilots to them.
Airline and charter pilots: the 61.57(e)(1)-(3) exceptions apply only while flying for that certificate holder. Renting a light airplane, they need 61.57 currency like anyone else.
Start every flight review or IPC by having the pilot do the 61.57 check out loud from their own logbook.
gaps: The sources do not say whether instrument tasks flown earlier in the month of the flight count toward that flight; FAA legal interpretations (not uploaded) address it.
InFO 15012 on logging instrument approaches (when an approach in actual conditions may be counted) is referenced by AC 61-98E but is not an uploaded source.
AC 61-136 and each ATD's Letter of Authorization are not in the sources; credit for a specific device must come from its LOA.
FAA legal interpretations on safety pilot logging and medical requirements are not in the sources; the lesson reads 61.51, 61.3 and 91.109 directly.
Not taught: the 61.57(e)(4) turbine multi-crew night alternative (multiengine), glider instrument currency (61.57(c)(3)) and night vision goggle currency (61.57(f)-(g)).

activities.title: True or false: passenger currency
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Three touch-and-goes in a tailwheel Piper Cub in the last 90 days let you take a passenger in the Cub.
cards.why: For a tailwheel airplane, the landings must be to a full stop in a tailwheel airplane [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)(ii)]].

cards.s: Landings in a Cessna 152 count toward passenger currency in a Cessna 172.
cards.why: For non-high-performance small aircraft the rule applies only to category and class, so a pilot current in a C152 is current in a C172 [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.3]].

cards.s: Landings your instructor made while you rode along count toward your currency.
cards.why: You must have acted as the sole manipulator of the flight controls [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)(i)]].

cards.s: If you are not 90-day current, you may fly with an instructor in training aimed only at getting current, as long as the two of you are the only people aboard.
cards.why: (a) and (b) do not apply to training limited to meeting them, when you and the instructor are the sole occupants [[60:242|14 CFR 61.57(e)(5)]].

cards.s: Any flight simulator may be used for the three takeoffs and landings.
cards.why: Only a FFS or FTD approved for landings and used in an approved Part 142 course [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(3)]].

cards.s: Instrument currency uses the same 90-day window as passenger currency.
cards.why: Instrument currency looks back 6 calendar months before the month of the flight [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]].

activities.title: Night landing: read the lights
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

pins.label: VASI all white: above glide path
VASI red over white: on glide path
Tire marks: begin the round out

activities.title: Count the clock
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Sunset is 7:48 pm. Your third full-stop landing was at 8:35 pm. How many more minutes would you have needed to wait for that landing to count toward night currency?
items.why: The window opens 1 hour after sunset: 7:48 + 1:00 = 8:48 pm. 8:48 - 8:35 = 13 minutes [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]].

items.q: Your 3 takeoffs and landings were on July 1. Today is September 20. How many days ago were they? (Within 90 means you may carry passengers.)
items.why: July 1 to August 1 is 31 days, August 1 to September 1 is 31, plus 19 more = 81 days, inside the preceding 90 days [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)]].

items.q: In the last 6 calendar months you logged 2 approaches under the hood with a safety pilot, 3 in an AATD (its LOA gives that credit; device, time and content recorded), and 1 you watched from the right seat as a friend's safety pilot. How many more approaches do you need?
items.why: 2 + 3 = 5 count [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(2)]]. The one you watched does not: you only log instrument time when you fly solely by instruments [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(1)]]. 6 - 5 = 1.

items.q: Your last approaches, holding and tracking were on February 14. Type the number (1 to 12) of the last month you may act as PIC under IFR without doing more.
items.why: August's window is February through July, so it still includes February. September's window starts in March. August = 8 [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]].

items.q: Same tasks, no more instrument flying. Type the number (1 to 12) of the last month you can regain IFR currency without an IPC.
items.why: Out from September 1. September through February is six calendar months; in March you are out more than six, so an IPC is required. February = 2 [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]].

activities.title: Does it count for IFR currency?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Approach in actual IMC as PIC, location and type logged
Approach under the hood in VMC, qualified safety pilot named in the log
Holding in an approved FTD representing an airplane, device, time and content recorded
Tracking a course in an AATD used as its LOA allows, with a record kept
Approach you watched from the right seat as safety pilot
Approach under the hood with a student pilot as safety pilot
Approach flown in March, for an IFR flight in October
Approaches in a helicopter, to keep airplane IFR privileges

activities.title: Which rule says that?
activities.intro: Tap a rule, then what it requires.

pairs.r: 3 takeoffs and landings in 90 days to carry persons
3 full-stop night landings, 1 hr after sunset to 1 hr before sunrise
6 approaches, holding, intercepting and tracking in 6 calendar months
IPC once more than 6 calendar months out of IFR currency
Log approach location, type and safety pilot name
Safety pilot required for simulated instrument flight

activities.title: Can I legally and safely fly tonight?
activities.intro: Today is Tuesday, October 20. You are a private pilot, airplane single-engine land, instrument rated, and you fly N123AB, a Cessna 172. Your logbook: 3 day full-stop landings on September 12; last night landings June 2; in March, 6 approaches with holding and tracking; in May, 4 more approaches with holding and tracking; nothing since. A friend wants to fly with you to dinner 80 NM away and back tonight. Sunset is 6:15 pm.

steps.s: Can you take your friend on the trip out this afternoon, day VFR?
options: No: you need landings within the last 30 days
Yes: the September 12 landings are 38 days ago, same category and class
No: you need a night landing first
Yes, but only if your friend is also a pilot
steps.why: 3 takeoffs and landings as sole manipulator within the preceding 90 days, same category and class [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)]]. September 12 to October 20 is 38 days.

steps.s: You plan to land back home at 8:30 pm with your friend aboard. Is that legal?
options: Yes: you are day current, and that is enough
Yes, if you land before civil twilight ends
No: your last night landings were June 2, and 8:30 pm is after 7:15 pm
No, unless you file IFR for the return
steps.why: From 1 hour after sunset (7:15 pm) you need 3 full-stop night takeoffs and landings in the preceding 90 days. June 2 is more than 90 days ago [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]].

steps.s: What is the best fix for tonight's trip?
options: Make 3 full-stop landings after 7:15 pm with your friend aboard, then fly on
Have your friend fly the landings while you log them
Count 3 landings made between sunset and 7:15 pm
Plan to be on the ground back home before 7:15 pm, or get night current solo on another evening first
steps.why: The rule bars carrying persons in that window until you are current, the landings must be yours as sole manipulator, and they only count after 1 hour past sunset [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]].

steps.s: You move the trip to Saturday, October 24. The return is forecast at 800 ft overcast. Are you IFR current?
options: Yes: you flew approaches in May, within six months
No: you need an IPC because March was more than six months ago
No: October's window is April to September and holds only 4 approaches; fly 2 more with a safety pilot, an instructor or a device
Yes: holding and tracking make up for the 2 missing approaches
steps.why: You need six approaches plus holding and tracking in the window [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]]. March's tasks covered you through September, so you have been out less than six calendar months and need no IPC yet [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]].

steps.s: Your friend, a private pilot ASEL with no instrument rating and a current medical, offers to be your safety pilot on Thursday in clear weather. What then?
options: Yes, she qualifies. Log each approach's location and type and her name as safety pilot
No: a safety pilot must hold an instrument rating
Yes, and nothing needs logging because it was VMC
No: only a CFII may watch currency approaches
steps.why: A safety pilot needs a private certificate with category and class ratings [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], and the log must show approach location, type and the safety pilot's name [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(3)]].

steps.s: Thursday goes well and you are IFR current. Saturday's return is still 800 ft overcast, at night. Your written night IFR minimum is a 999 ft ceiling, and you have not flown in actual IMC for a year. Best decision?
options: Go: you are legal, so personal minimums don't matter
Lower your minimum to 800 ft just for this trip
Go, and drop below the clouds VFR if it gets bad
Stay with your minimums: plan a day return, drive, or reschedule
steps.why: Don't adjust personal minimums to complete a specific flight; written minimums make the no-go decision easier [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. Rated but not proficient pilots are at risk of loss of control in IMC [[15:12|AC 61-98E 2.1.5]].

final_quiz.q: You are 90-day current in a Cessna 172. A friend offers his Piper Archer, also single-engine land and not high performance. May you take a passenger in it today?
options: Yes by the rule, though the FAA recommends a checkout and currency in that make and model
No: passenger currency is by make and model
No: you need 3 landings in an Archer first by rule
Only with an instructor aboard
final_quiz.why: The basic currency rule applies to category and class only, but the FAA recommends currency and a checkout in each make and model [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.3]] [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: Sunset is 5:20 pm. You are not night current. You will land with a passenger at 6:05 pm. What applies?
options: Not legal: it is after sunset
Not legal: it is after civil twilight
Legal for currency, since the night window starts at 6:20 pm, but position lights must be on
Legal, and position lights are not needed until 6:20 pm
final_quiz.why: 61.57(b) applies from 1 hour after sunset [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]]. Position lights are required from sunset to sunrise [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: On August 1 you made 3 full-stop landings at 9:30 pm; sunset was 8:20 pm. Today is October 15. May you carry passengers tonight after dark?
options: No: night landings expire after 60 days
Yes: 75 days ago, full stops, more than 1 hour after sunset
No: 9:30 pm was less than 1 hour after sunset
No: night landings must be within the last 30 days
final_quiz.why: 9:30 pm is after 9:20 pm, and August 1 to October 15 is 75 days, within the preceding 90 [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: Sunset is 7:00 pm and civil twilight ends at 7:28 pm. You make 3 full-stop landings at 7:45 pm. What do they give you?
options: Night currency and night time
Night currency but no night time
Neither night time nor night currency
Night time to log, but no night currency
final_quiz.why: After civil twilight ends is night for logging [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]], but currency landings must be from 1 hour after sunset, here 8:00 pm [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: It is November 10. You logged 6 approaches in June, holding in July, and course tracking in an ATD in September, with the device, time and content recorded. May you act as PIC under IFR today?
options: No: tracking must be done in an airplane
No: an instructor had to sign the ATD session
No: all three tasks must be on one flight
Yes, if the ATD's LOA gives that credit; all tasks fall in May to October
final_quiz.why: Any combination of aircraft and devices may be used [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(2)]], ATD credit follows its LOA [[15:21|AC 61-98E 3.2]], and a device record is enough for currency [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(5)]].

final_quiz.q: Your IFR currency ran out at the end of April. It is September. What are your options?
options: You must take an IPC
Do the six approaches, holding and tracking with a safety pilot, an instructor or a device
File IFR alone on a clear day and log the approaches as PIC
Wait for October, when the window resets
final_quiz.why: May through September is not more than six calendar months, so no IPC yet [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(1)]]. You may not act as PIC under IFR until the tasks are done [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]].

final_quiz.q: Your club's CFI has an instrument rating on his pilot certificate but no instrument rating on his flight instructor certificate. Can he give your IPC in the club's 172?
options: Yes: any CFI may give an IPC
Yes, if the IPC is done in an AATD
No: he needs the instrument rating on his flight instructor certificate too
No: only an examiner may give an IPC
final_quiz.why: The instructor must hold an instrument rating on both the pilot and flight instructor certificates for the category and class used [[15:30|AC 61-98E 5.1.1]]. Authorized instructors may give IPCs [[60:240|14 CFR 61.57(d)(3)]].

final_quiz.q: You plan hood work in a Cessna 172. Which is required by 91.109(c)?
options: An instrument-rated safety pilot
Dual controls and a private pilot ASEL safety pilot with adequate vision
An IFR flight plan
A CFII aboard
final_quiz.why: 91.109(c) requires a safety pilot with at least a private certificate and category and class ratings, adequate vision forward and to each side, and dual controls [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]] [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)-(3)]].

final_quiz.q: You fly as safety pilot (not PIC) for a friend under the hood. You hold a private certificate, airplane single-engine land. What may you log?
options: Instrument time, because the flight was simulated IFR
PIC time, because you watch for traffic
Nothing at all
SIC time, because the regulations require a second pilot for this flight
final_quiz.why: SIC may be logged when you hold the category and class rating and the regulations under which the flight is conducted require more than one pilot [[60:229|14 CFR 61.51(f)(2)]]. Instrument time is only for the pilot flying by instruments [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: You finish 6 approaches, holding and tracking in the airplane on June 20. What is the last day you may act as PIC under IFR without doing more?
options: December 20
December 31
November 30
June 20 of the next year
final_quiz.why: December's window is June through November, so it includes June. January's starts in July. So you are current through December 31 [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: On Monday you make 3 full-stop landings in a tailwheel Citabria. Can you take a passenger in a nosewheel Cessna 172 on Tuesday?
options: Yes: same category and class
No: tailwheel landings don't count for nosewheel airplanes
No: you need 3 more in the 172 itself
Only by day with an instructor aboard
final_quiz.why: The rule asks for the same category, class and type (if required), and adds the tailwheel condition only when the airplane to be flown has a tailwheel [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(a)(1)(ii)]].

final_quiz.q: According to the RMH, when is the right time to change your personal minimums?
options: The morning of a trip, based on the forecast
In flight, when the weather turns out worse
When time and objectivity allow an honest review, not under pressure to fly
Whenever passengers are waiting
final_quiz.why: Do not adjust personal minimums to complete a specific flight. Consider changes when there is time for an honest self-analysis, one variable at a time [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

final_quiz.q: You meet every 61.57 requirement, but lately you have flown only on light-wind days at a 7,000-ft runway. Saturday's plan: gusty crosswind at a 2,800-ft runway with passengers. What does AC 61-98E suggest?
options: Get more takeoff and landing practice in stronger winds and on short runways before carrying passengers in those conditions
You are current, so go
Practice solo that morning while the passengers wait
Ask ATC for a longer runway once you arrive
final_quiz.why: The FAA says to treat 61.57(a) and (b) as minimums and get more experience in stronger winds or at short runways before carrying passengers in similar conditions [[15:20|AC 61-98E 3.1.1]].
